title: Why does naive `hash(key) % N` sharding make rebalancing painful (changing N remaps most keys), and how does consistent hashing (with virtual nodes) reduce the data movement when shards are added/removed?
shortTitle: Why does naive hash(key) % N sharding make rebalancing painful, and how does consistent hashing help
keyPoints: hash(key) % N bakes the shard count into every key assignment, so changing N remaps nearly every key.
Going from 4 to 5 shards relocates roughly 80% of all data, a catastrophic migration.
Consistent hashing maps keys and shards onto a fixed ring and assigns each key to the next shard clockwise.
Adding a shard moves only about 1/N of keys from the one adjacent shard, not the whole dataset.
Virtual nodes place each physical shard at many ring positions to even out distribution.
Virtual nodes also spread rebalancing load across many shards instead of dumping it on one neighbor.
Rebalancing should run in the background with throttling so it does not overwhelm the cluster.

s1_definition.oneliner: With hash modulo N, changing N remaps almost every key so rebalancing moves nearly all data, while consistent hashing on a ring moves only about a 1/N slice when a shard is added or removed, and virtual nodes keep that movement even.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Modulo sharding** – `shard = hash(key) % N` distributes keys evenly for a fixed N, but changing N changes the result for almost every key, forcing a near-total data migration.
- **Consistent hashing** – keys and shards are mapped onto a fixed circular ring; each key belongs to the next shard clockwise, so adding or removing a shard moves only the keys in one arc (roughly 1/N).
- **Virtual nodes** – each physical shard occupies many points on the ring, evening out arc sizes and spreading rebalancing load across many shards instead of one neighbor.
- **Rebalancing** – data movement during shard changes should be throttled and run in the background to avoid overwhelming the cluster.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India assigns each customer to a counter by taking a number and dividing by the number of counters. If the bank opens one more counter, the divisor changes, so almost every customer is reassigned and everyone has to move their files. Consistent hashing arranges counters around a round table and seats each customer at the next counter clockwise. Adding a counter steals customers from only one slice of the table. Giving each counter several seats around the table (virtual nodes) keeps the crowd evenly spread.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Modulo: hash(key) % N
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  N=4: key -> shard 1                  │
  │  N=5: key -> shard 3  (MOVED!)        │
  │  ~80% of keys change shard            │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Consistent Hash Ring (virtual nodes)
        ┌─── shard-A-vn0
       /
  0 ──●── shard-B-vn2
  │     \
  │      ●── key:SAV2001 → walks CW → shard-B
  │     /
  │   ●── shard-C-vn1
  │  /
  MAX ── shard-A-vn1  (wraps around)

  Adding shard-D:
  Only keys in shard-D's new arc move.
  All other keys stay on their current shard.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Modulo sharding assigns keys with `hash(key) % N` and gives an even spread for a fixed cluster, but it is fragile because N is baked into the formula. Changing N when you add or remove a shard remaps nearly every key, forcing a massive data migration that saturates the network and risks inconsistency. For a large bank that turns scaling out, which should be routine, into a rare and dangerous event.

Consistent hashing solves this by mapping both keys and shards onto a fixed ring. A key belongs to the next shard clockwise, so adding a shard moves only the keys in one arc, roughly 1/N of the total. Virtual nodes place each physical shard at many ring positions to even out the distribution and spread the rebalancing load across many neighbors instead of dumping it on one. At National Bank of India, Pankaj replaced modulo sharding with a consistent hash ring after a fifth-shard migration remapped almost every customer, and subsequent shard additions moved only a small fraction of data with zero service interruption.

The key discipline is to use consistent hashing from the start, choose a number of virtual nodes that balances smoothness against metadata size, throttle rebalancing data in the background, and remember that consistent hashing handles placement but not replication, so you still replicate each key to several successive shards on the ring for availability.

Remember one sentence: hash modulo N bakes the shard count into every key so changing N remaps nearly everything, whereas consistent hashing with virtual nodes moves only about 1/N of keys by walking the ring clockwise.
